To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have created a set of open and reproducible pipelines that can be used to analyze tumor exome and transcriptomic data to create integrated cancer genome profiles that can then be used to identify mutations that may be associated with cancer and potential drugs for treatment.

we developed three open, reproducible, integrated pipelines for analyzing exome and transcriptomic data from cancer samples and applied the pipelines to find differences between pancreatic cancer cell lines and tumors.

the exome and transcriptomes of pancreatic cancer cell lines and tumors are similar, but that the tumors contain more deleterious mutations in highly expressed genes and more druggable mutations than the cell lines.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of reproducible, open pipelines to create an integrated tumor profile and use the profile for finding relevant mutations in the context of drug development.
the development of open, reproducible, distributed pipelines that can be applied to cancer exome and RNA‐seq data and used to find relevant mutations in primary tumors and potentially useful drugs.
the development of open pipelines that can be used to analyze cancer genome sequence data and identify potentially actionable mutations in cancer patients.

the exome analysis of the cell line data is more complete than the primary tumor data, but the transcriptome analysis shows the opposite.
our pipeline has been able to identify several mutations in the primary tumors that have been reported in cell lines, but that are absent in the primary tumors.
our pipelines can be used to identify potential therapeutic targets and drugs in cancer, and that the results of our analyses are consistent with published results.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have created an integrated, open‐source pipeline for analyzing whole exome, whole transcriptome, and targeted exome data to identify mutations in primary tumors and cell lines that can be used to find potential drugs.
we have found a set of mutations that are common to pancreatic cancer tumors and cancer cell lines, but also found mutations that are unique to tumors or unique to cancer cell lines.
our pipelines can be used to identify potential drug targets in cancer patients and to compare the genomes of primary tumors and cancer cell lines.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the pipelines can be used to identify mutations and potential drug targets in a clinical setting.
we have created open, reproducible tools that can be applied to any cancer and that can be used to find similarities and differences between cell lines and primary tumor data.
we can use the pipelines to find similarities and differences between cancer cell lines and tumors.
